title: Reachability, Latency & Path
sub: Measure whether a host answers, how long it takes, where the packets travel and how big they can be
goals: Read ping output and statistics and explain every number in them
Use traceroute and mtr to locate where on a path latency or loss starts
Compute average, jitter, loss and 95th percentile of round-trip times with awk
Find the path MTU to a host with ping and the Don't Fragment bit
Build latency-log, a script that records round-trip times to CSV and summarises them

blocks.text: [Chapter 12](#net-local) was about what your Mac is. This chapter is about whether it can *reach* something else, how quickly, and by which route. The tools are small and old (`ping` dates from 1983) but they answer the first question in every network investigation: is the problem here, at the next hop, or far away? You will send probes, learn how the probes work so you can interpret the silence as well as the answers, and finish with `latency-log`, a recorder you can leave running while you work.

blocks.title: Probe only what you own or may test

blocks.text: `ping`, `traceroute` and `mtr` send real packets to other machines. Use your own Mac, your LAN, `localhost`, your lab host `{{labhost}}`, and well-known public services such as `example.com` or `1.1.1.1` at low rates. Do not point sweeps or high-rate pings at networks you do not own or have permission to test.
How ping works

`ping` sends an **ICMP echo request** (type 8) to a host. A host that is up, reachable and willing replies with an **ICMP echo reply** (type 0), copying the request's payload back. `ping` records the time between sending and receiving; that is the **round-trip time (RTT)**. ICMP is carried directly inside IP, with no ports: it is not TCP or UDP, which is why `ping` works as a test of the network layer alone.

blocks.code:
your Mac                                                   target
  ┌─────────┐   echo request  type 8, seq=0, 56 data bytes   ┌─────────┐
  │  ping   │ ───────────────────────────────────────────▶   │ kernel  │
  │         │                                                │ answers │
  │  timer  │ ◀───────────────────────────────────────────   │ itself  │
  └─────────┘   echo reply    type 0, seq=0, same payload    └─────────┘
      RTT = reply arrival time - request send time
      (the target's kernel replies, no application is involved)

blocks.text: Because the *kernel* of the target replies, a good ping proves the host is up and the path works in both directions, and says nothing about whether any service (web, SSH) on it is working.

blocks.code:
$ ping -c 3 192.168.1.1
PING 192.168.1.1 (192.168.1.1): 56 data bytes
64 bytes from 192.168.1.1: icmp_seq=0 ttl=64 time=2.100 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.1.1: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=2.470 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.1.1: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=1.890 ms

--- 192.168.1.1 ping statistics ---
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0.0% packet loss
round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 1.890/2.153/2.470/0.240 ms

blocks.text: Reading one reply line

tokens.exp: size of the ICMP message: 56 data bytes plus the 8-byte ICMP header (the IP header is not counted)
the sequence number; starts at 0 on macOS, so a gap means a lost probe
the TTL the reply had on arrival, after losing one per router on the way back

blocks.title: Extracting the time from a reply line

tokens.exp: pipe the text lines into awk
field separator is a regular expression: either "=" or a space
run the action only on lines containing "time="
print the second-to-last field; NF is the field count, and the last field is "ms"

blocks.text: The `ttl` value is a clue to distance. Hosts start replies from a round number: 64 (macOS, Linux, most routers), 128 (Windows) or 255 (many network devices). A reply that arrives with `ttl=56` probably started at 64, so it crossed about 8 routers on the way back. A reply from your gateway with `ttl=64` crossed none.
The summary at the end

blocks.code:
--- example.com ping statistics ---
10 packets transmitted, 9 packets received, 10.0% packet loss
round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 11.205/12.939/16.102/1.535 ms

items.text: **Packet loss** is the fraction of probes with no reply. Occasional single losses are normal on Wi-Fi and busy paths. Sustained loss above 1 to 2 percent is a problem; 100 percent means either no path or a host that ignores ICMP.
**min/avg/max** show the spread. A min close to the average and a high max means occasional spikes (queues, Wi-Fi retries). A high min means the whole path is slow.
**stddev** is the standard deviation of the RTTs, which you can read as a rough **jitter**. Linux calls the same field `mdev`.

blocks.text: When there is no answer, macOS prints `Request timeout for icmp_seq 5` and the probe counts as lost. Hosts can drop ICMP on purpose; firewalls and cloud hosts often do. A ping that fails does not prove the host is down. Confirm with a TCP test such as `nc -z -w 3 host 443` or `curl -sI host`, covered in [Ports and services](#ports).

blocks.name: ping
blocks.sum: Send ICMP echo requests to a host and report replies, round-trip times and loss.
blocks.syntax: ping [-c count] [-i seconds] [-s bytes] [-t timeout] [-W ms] [-D] [-n] [-q] [-o] [-S src] [-b iface] host

how.text: `ping` opens an ICMP socket (the binary is installed with the privilege it needs, so you do not run it as root), sends one echo request per interval, each with an incrementing sequence number and a timestamp in the payload, and prints a line for each reply. When you press Ctrl-C, or when `-c` probes are done, it prints the statistics.

The exit status is useful in scripts: **0** means at least one reply came back, **2** means the packets were sent but nothing answered, and any other value (for example **68**, "unknown host") means an error such as a name that does not resolve.

flags.d: Stop after N probes. Without it, `ping` runs until Ctrl-C.
Seconds between probes (default 1). Fractions work; intervals below 0.1 s need root on macOS.
Size of the data part. Default 56. Used with `-D` for MTU discovery.
Exit after s **seconds** in total, whatever has been received. A script's safety net.
How long to wait for each reply, in **milliseconds** on macOS (it is seconds on Linux).
Set the Don't Fragment bit in the IP header.
Numeric output only; do not resolve names for replies.
Quiet: print only the header and the summary.
Exit successfully after the first reply. A fast "is it up?" check.
Use this source address, which must be one of your own. Useful when you have several.
Send out of the named interface (macOS addition).

examples.out:
PING example.com (93.184.216.34): 56 data bytes
64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=0 ttl=56 time=11.842 ms
64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=1 ttl=56 time=12.310 ms
64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=2 ttl=56 time=11.205 ms
64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=3 ttl=56 time=14.987 ms

--- example.com ping statistics ---
4 packets transmitted, 4 packets received, 0.0% packet loss
round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 11.205/12.586/14.987/1.441 ms

examples.desc: A quick up-or-down test for a script

anat.exp: flag: four probes, then print statistics
target: a name or an address

examples.desc: Just the time values, one per line

gotchas: `-W` is milliseconds on macOS and seconds on Linux. A copied Linux command with `-W 2` waits two milliseconds here and reports everything as lost. Use `-W 2000`.
With `-c 1` and a dead host, `ping` can wait a long time before giving up. Add `-t 2` so it always returns.
Short intervals send faster than most links want. Keep `-i` at 0.2 or more unless you are testing your own gear.

blocks.text: Why ICMP deserves respect
ICMP is not only echo. It is how IP reports problems, and each message type teaches you something about the path.

head: Type
Name
When you see it
rows: code 0 network, 1 host, 3 port, 4 fragmentation needed but DF set, 13 administratively prohibited
a router tells you a better first hop exists
a router decremented TTL to 0 (code 0); the basis of `traceroute`

blocks.text: Types 3 and 11 matter most here. Type 11 is how `traceroute` finds each router. Type 3 code 4 is how path MTU discovery works, and its absence is a classic cause of connections that hang on large transfers.
Latency, jitter, loss and bandwidth
These four words are often mixed up. They are independent, and a connection can be good at one and poor at another.

head: Metric
What it measures
Typical good values
Hurts
rows: time for a packet to go there and back
under 5 ms on a LAN, 10 to 40 ms to a nearby service, 100+ ms across oceans
variation of latency between consecutive packets
probes that never get a reply
everything, because TCP retransmits and slows down
how many bits per second the link can carry

blocks.text: A fast link (high bandwidth) can still feel slow if its RTT is high, because each request waits a full round trip: loading a page that needs 30 sequential requests at 100 ms RTT takes 3 seconds before any data transfer time. Distance sets a floor: light in fibre travels about 200 km per millisecond, so 1000 km costs at least 5 ms each way.
Jitter has several definitions. A simple one for scripts is the **mean absolute difference between consecutive RTTs**, which you can compute from a ping log with `awk` in a few lines.

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ awk -F'[= ]' '/time=/ {print $(NF-1)}' ping.log
11.842
12.310
11.205
14.987
12.044
13.551
11.930
16.102
12.477
$ awk -F'[= ]' '/time=/ {t=$(NF-1); if (n++) {d=t-prev; if (d<0) d=-d; s+=d}; prev=t} END {printf "jitter=%.3f ms\n", s/(n-1)}' ping.log
jitter=2.403 ms

blocks.text: The first command shows the pipeline stage you will reuse all chapter: split each line on `=` and spaces, and the second-to-last field is the number of milliseconds, because the line ends with the word `ms`. The second command is the jitter formula: remember the previous time, add the absolute difference, divide by one less than the number of samples.
Statistics from a ping log
`ping.log` in your lab is a saved `ping -c 10` run with one lost probe. It is a good dataset for the shape every latency report takes: **extract the numbers, then reduce them.**

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ awk '/packet loss/ {print $7}' ping.log
10.0%
$ grep -c 'Request timeout' ping.log
1
$ awk -F'[= ]' '/time=/ {t=$(NF-1); s+=t; n++; if (min==""||t<min) min=t; if (t>max) max=t} END {printf "n=%d min=%.3f avg=%.3f max=%.3f\n", n, min, s/n, max}' ping.log
n=9 min=11.205 avg=12.939 max=16.102

blocks.text: The `awk` reducer keeps four variables: a running sum, a count, a minimum and a maximum. Because awk variables start empty, `min==""` is the "first sample" test. This is the template for every statistic in the chapter.
Percentiles need sorting

An average hides spikes. The **95th percentile (p95)** answers "95 percent of the probes were at or below this time", and it is how latency is usually reported. To compute it with the **nearest-rank** method, sort the values and take the one at position ceil(0.95 × n).

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ awk -F'[= ]' '/time=/ {print $(NF-1)}' ping.log | sort -n | awk '{v[NR]=$1} END {p=int(0.95*NR); if (p<0.95*NR) p++; print "p95 =", v[p]}'
p95 = 16.102

blocks.text: Read it as two programs: the first `awk` extracts, `sort -n` orders numerically, and the second `awk` stores every value in an array indexed by line number. `END` runs after the last line, when `NR` holds the count. The `int(...)` followed by a conditional increment is how you round up in awk, which has no `ceil`.
`sort` without `-n` compares text, so `9.5` sorts after `12.3` because `9` is greater than `1`. Any pipeline that sorts numbers needs `sort -n`, or `sort -g` for floating point with exponents.
Recipes: ping in a pipeline
These are the shapes you will reuse. Each is one sentence of purpose plus a pipeline.

**Ping every host in `hosts.txt` and rank by average RTT.** Loop with `while read`, capture the average, print it with the name, sort numerically. Hosts that do not answer get `9999` so they sort last.

blocks.code:
while read -r h; do
  avg=$(ping -c 3 -t 4 -W 1000 "$h" 2>/dev/null | awk -F/ '/round-trip/ {print $5}')
  print "${avg:-9999} $h"
done < hosts.txt | sort -n

blocks.text: **Timestamp every reply.** A pipe into a `while read` loop lets you prepend anything to each line. This gives you a log you can line up with other events.

blocks.code: ping -c 10 {{host}} | while IFS= read -r line; do print "$(date '+%H:%M:%S') $line"; done

blocks.text: **Alert when a reply is slow.** `-v max=50` passes a value into awk as a variable. The pattern selects reply lines whose time exceeds it, and the action prints the sequence number (field 6 after splitting on `=` and spaces) and the time.

blocks.code: ping -c 20 {{host}} | awk -F'[= ]' -v max=50 '/time=/ && $(NF-1) > max {print "SLOW", $(NF-1), "ms at seq", $6}'

blocks.text: **Sweep a /24 for live hosts.** `seq` generates the last octet, `xargs -P` runs many pings in parallel, and a successful ping prints its address. Sixty-four at a time finishes in a few seconds. Run it only on your own LAN. Change `192.168.1` to the first three octets of your subnet.

A side effect is useful: every host that answered is now in your ARP cache, so `arp -an` immediately after the sweep lists devices that did not answer ping but did answer ARP (many phones and printers block ICMP and still answer ARP). That is the idea behind `lan-inventory`, which you started in [See your own network](#net-local).

blocks.title: Why ARP finds more than ping

blocks.text: A host on your subnet must answer ARP for traffic to reach it at all; a firewall that blocks ICMP does not stop ARP. After a sweep, run `arp -an | grep -v incomplete`. Hosts that appear with a MAC but did not print in the sweep are alive and filtering ping.
TTL and traceroute

Every IP packet has a **TTL** (time to live) field. Each router decrements it by one and drops the packet when it reaches zero, sending back an ICMP *time exceeded* message from its own address. The design protects against routing loops. `traceroute` turns the safety mechanism into a map by sending probes with TTL 1, 2, 3 and so on, and collecting the replies.

blocks.code:
TTL=1  ──▶ [router 1] ✗ TTL hits 0 ──▶ "time exceeded" from router 1 address
  TTL=2  ──▶ [router 1] ──▶ [router 2] ✗ ──▶ "time exceeded" from router 2 address
  TTL=3  ──▶ [router 1] ──▶ [router 2] ──▶ [router 3] ✗ ──▶ ... from router 3
  TTL=4  ──▶ [router 1] ──▶ [router 2] ──▶ [router 3] ──▶ [destination]
                                                            │
        UDP probes: destination answers "port unreachable" (type 3 code 3) ◀┘
        ICMP probes (-I): destination answers "echo reply"

blocks.text: By default macOS `traceroute` sends **UDP** datagrams to a high port starting at 33434. Routers on the way answer with *time exceeded*; the destination, which has nothing listening there, answers *port unreachable*, which tells `traceroute` it has arrived. With `-I` it sends ICMP echo requests instead, which more networks permit.
Reading it:

items.text: Each line is one hop: the hop number, then the address (or name) of the router that answered, then the RTT of each of the three probes (`-q 3` by default).
**Hop 1** is your gateway, `192.168.1.1`. Hops 2 to 5 are your ISP's network. A private address like `10.34.0.1` at hop 2 is normal inside an ISP.

**Hop 4 shows `* * *`.** No reply within the 5 second wait. That is often not a fault: many routers forward traffic perfectly well but are configured not to send time-exceeded messages, or rate-limit them. If later hops answer, as hop 5 does, the path is fine.

**Hop 6 jumps from 11 ms to 96 ms and stays high through the destination.** A *persistent* jump marks a long link (a transatlantic hop, a congested peering point). A spike at one hop that disappears at the next means that router was slow to *answer* ICMP, not slow to *forward*.
The path shown is the path **to** the destination. The reply path can differ (asymmetric routing), so a bad hop might be on the way back.

blocks.name: traceroute
blocks.sum: Show the routers between you and a destination by sending probes with increasing TTL.
blocks.syntax: traceroute [-I] [-n] [-m max_ttl] [-q nqueries] [-w seconds] [-P proto] [-a] [-f first_ttl] [-S] host

how.text: `traceroute` sends groups of probes, three per TTL value by default. Each router that discards a probe returns an ICMP *time exceeded* message whose source address identifies that hop, and the program prints the time between sending the probe and receiving that message. It stops when the destination answers or when `-m` (maximum hops, 64 by default on macOS) is reached.

Per-hop times are not independent measurements of that link. They include the router's own delay in generating the message, which can be slow because it is done by the router's control plane. Compare the *trend* across hops rather than one number.

flags.d: Do not resolve addresses to names. Much faster, and avoids confusing reverse-DNS names.
Maximum number of hops (TTL) to try.
Probes per hop (default 3). `-q 1` is faster and easier to parse.
Seconds to wait for each reply (default 5). Lower it to finish faster when hops are silent.
Use ICMP echo instead of UDP probes.
Probe protocol: `udp`, `tcp`, `icmp` and others by name or number.
Start at TTL N, skipping the first N-1 hops (for example `-f 2` to skip your own router).
Look up the autonomous-system number for each hop.
Print a summary of unanswered probes per hop.

examples.desc: Trace the path numerically with ICMP probes
Fast, parseable trace: one probe per hop, short wait

anat.exp: wait at most 2 seconds per probe

examples.desc: The list of hop addresses, one per line (a `*` marks a silent hop)
Find the hop where RTT jumps the most
examples.code: traceroute -n -q 1 -w 2 {{host}} | awk '$3+0>0 {d=$3-prev; if (d>maxd) {maxd=d; hop=$1" "$2}; prev=$3} END {print "largest jump:", maxd, "ms at hop", hop}'

gotchas: `* * *` is not proof of a fault. Trust the pattern: if nothing answers after some hop to the end, the path is blocked there; if later hops answer, the silent router merely ignores ICMP.
Some networks drop UDP probes but allow ICMP. If the default trace dies early, try `-I`; if ICMP mode reports a permission error on your system, run it with `sudo`.
notes: Annotations after a time such as `!H` (host unreachable), `!N` (network unreachable), `!X` (administratively prohibited) or `!` alone mean the reply carried an error or an unusual TTL. `man traceroute` lists them.

blocks.text: IPv6 has its own binaries on macOS: `ping6` and `traceroute6`, used like their IPv4 counterparts, for example `ping6 -c 3 2606:4700:4700::1111`. They are separate commands, not flags. If a site resolves to both address families, `ping` and `traceroute` use IPv4 and the `6` variants use IPv6, so test both when something is slow only on one.
Parsing a trace
`traceroute -n -q 1` prints one probe per hop, which makes each line a fixed shape: hop number, address, time. Pipelines get easy.

blocks.code:
$ traceroute -n -q 1 -w 2 example.com | awk '{print $2}'
192.168.1.1
10.34.0.1
81.139.72.5
*
62.172.103.40
203.0.113.9
93.184.216.34
$ traceroute -n -q 1 -w 2 example.com | awk '$3+0>0 {d=$3-prev; if (d>maxd) {maxd=d; hop=$1" "$2}; prev=$3} END {print "largest jump:", maxd, "ms at hop", hop}'
largest jump: 85.375 ms at hop 6 203.0.113.9

blocks.text: The second command ignores silent hops (their third field is not a number), keeps the previous hop's time, and remembers the hop with the greatest increase. It is a one-line answer to "where did it get slow", and it matches what you read by eye above.
mtr: ping and traceroute together

`mtr` (my traceroute) runs a traceroute continuously, sending many probes to every hop, and shows loss and latency statistics per hop. One trace is a single snapshot; `mtr` shows the pattern over time, which is what you need to catch a congested or lossy link.

blocks.code: brew install mtr

blocks.title: mtr needs root and a path entry

blocks.text: `mtr` opens raw sockets, so it must run as root: `sudo mtr ...`. Homebrew installs it into `/opt/homebrew/sbin`, which `brew shellenv` adds to your `PATH` (see [Setup](#setup)). If `sudo mtr` says command not found, `sudo` is using a restricted path; run it with the full path, `sudo /opt/homebrew/sbin/mtr ...`.
How to read the report:

items.text: **Loss%** is per hop. Look at the **last** hop first. If the final hop shows 0 percent, the loss at hop 4 and hop 5 is routers refusing to answer probes, not lost traffic: your packets to hop 7 all got through.
Loss that **starts at one hop and continues to every later hop** is real. That is where traffic is being dropped.
**Snt** is probes sent; **Last, Avg, Best, Wrst** are in milliseconds; **StDev** is the spread, a jitter estimate.
A large **Wrst** next to a small **Avg** means rare spikes. A jump in **Avg** between hops that persists is the long link, as in traceroute.

blocks.name: mtr
blocks.sum: Continuously probe every hop on the path and report loss and latency statistics per hop.
blocks.syntax: sudo mtr [-r] [-w] [-n] [-c count] [-i seconds] [-T] [-P port] [-u] [-b] [-4|-6] host

how.text: `mtr` combines `traceroute` and `ping`. It first discovers the path with increasing TTL, then keeps sending probes to every hop in parallel, updating loss and latency statistics as replies arrive. In its interactive display (just `sudo mtr host`) the numbers update live; press `q` to quit. In **report mode** (`-r`) it sends `-c` rounds, prints a table and exits, which is what you capture into a file or paste into a support ticket.
By default `mtr` sends ICMP echo probes. When ICMP is filtered on the path, `-T` (TCP) with `-P 443` sends TCP SYN probes to a port that is allowed, and often gets a clearer picture.

flags.d: Report mode: run `-c` rounds, print a table, exit.
Wide report: do not truncate host names.
Numeric: skip reverse-DNS lookups.
Number of rounds (probes per hop) to send.
Seconds between rounds (default 1).
Use TCP SYN probes instead of ICMP (combine with `-P port`).
Use UDP probes.
Show both hostnames and IP addresses.
Force IPv4 or IPv6.

examples.desc: Probe with TCP port 443 when ICMP is filtered

anat.exp: report mode, wide, numeric, 20 rounds (flags can be bundled)

examples.desc: Which hops lose packets, with their loss percentage

gotchas: Loss at an intermediate hop that does not continue to the last hop is ICMP rate limiting. Judge by the last hop.
`sudo mtr` can fail with "command not found" because `sudo` resets `PATH`. Use `sudo /opt/homebrew/sbin/mtr`.
notes: Column positions differ with options like `-b`. Print the report once and count columns before you trust an `awk` field number.

blocks.text: Other probes exist for special cases. `nping` (part of the `nmap` package) and `hping3` craft custom probes such as TCP SYN pings, and `arping` (`brew install arping`) pings at the ARP layer, which works even when ICMP is blocked. They are optional and used in [Ports and services](#ports); the three tools above cover nearly all daily work.
MTU: how big can a packet be

Every link has a **maximum transmission unit (MTU)**, the largest IP packet it carries. Ethernet is 1500 bytes. VPNs, PPPoE (a common DSL encapsulation) and tunnels add headers and therefore have smaller MTUs (1492, 1420, 1380 are common). If a packet is larger than a link's MTU, a router either **fragments** it into pieces or, if the packet has the **Don't Fragment (DF)** bit set, drops it and sends back ICMP type 3 code 4 (*fragmentation needed*) with the MTU it could take. TCP sets DF on its segments and relies on those ICMP messages to learn the **path MTU**. Firewalls that drop all ICMP break that mechanism, and large transfers then stall while small ones work: the "MTU black hole".
You can find the path MTU with `ping -D -s SIZE`. The `-s` value is the **data** size. The IP packet is that plus 8 bytes of ICMP header plus 20 bytes of IP header, 28 bytes in all.

blocks.code:
IP packet limit (MTU)            1500
   - IP header                       -20
   - ICMP header                      -8
   ------------------------------------
   largest ping payload              1472     ping -D -s 1472 host

blocks.title: Measuring the largest packet that fits

tokens.exp: a single probe is enough for a yes/no answer
set the Don't Fragment bit, so a too-big packet is dropped instead of split
data bytes; with 28 bytes of headers this makes a 1500-byte packet
give up after 3 seconds in total

blocks.code:
$ ping -c 1 -D -s 1472 example.com
PING example.com (93.184.216.34): 1472 data bytes
1480 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=0 ttl=56 time=12.9 ms

$ ping -c 1 -D -s 1473 example.com
PING example.com (93.184.216.34): 1473 data bytes
ping: sendto: Message too long

--- example.com ping statistics ---
1 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100.0% packet loss

blocks.text: The second run fails locally because 1473 + 28 = 1501 exceeds your own interface's MTU. When the limit is further along the path, you instead get a timeout or an ICMP error, depending on whether the router sends the message. The largest size that works, plus 28, is your path MTU. A loop makes the search automatic:

blocks.code:
host={{host}}
for size in 1472 1452 1432 1412 1392 1372 1272; do
  if ping -c 1 -D -s $size -t 3 -W 1500 $host > /dev/null 2>&1; then
    print "payload $size works: path MTU is $(( size + 28 ))"
    break
  else
    print "payload $size fails"
  fi
done

blocks.text: If 1472 works, you have a standard 1500-byte path. If only a smaller size works, a tunnel or PPPoE link is reducing it, and your VPN or router may need an explicit MSS clamp or MTU setting.

Fragmentation moves work to routers and to the receiver, and a single lost fragment loses the whole packet. Modern stacks avoid it with path MTU discovery: send with DF set, shrink on ICMP feedback. IPv6 routers do not fragment at all; the sender must discover the path MTU, so a filtered ICMPv6 "packet too big" message causes the same black hole more severely.
networkQuality: bandwidth and responsiveness

Apple ships a speed test, `networkQuality` (macOS 12 and later). It measures **capacity** (upload and download throughput) and a newer metric, **responsiveness**: how many round trips per minute the connection can complete *while it is saturated*. A line can have high capacity and low responsiveness if its buffers fill under load (bufferbloat), which is what makes a video call stutter when someone starts a download.

blocks.name: networkQuality
blocks.sum: Measure upload and download capacity, idle latency and responsiveness under load, using Apple's test servers.

how.text: `networkQuality` downloads and uploads data from an Apple-run server while also measuring round-trip latency, in parallel by default or one direction at a time with `-s`. It reports how fast the link is, how long a single idle round trip takes, and the **responsiveness** score in round-trips per minute (RPM): above about 1000 RPM is good, below 200 will make interactive use feel sluggish under load.

The test deliberately saturates the connection for around 20 seconds, so run it when you are not in a call. The text layout of the report has changed between macOS releases and shows capacity as `Downlink capacity` and `Uplink capacity` in newer versions.

flags.d: Run upload and download sequentially rather than at the same time.
Verbose: more detail about each measurement.
Computer-readable output (JSON) for scripts.
Bind the test to an interface, for example `en0`, to compare Wi-Fi with Ethernet.
Use a different configuration URL (for a self-hosted server).
Use iCloud Private Relay for the test.
Disable certificate validation.
Connect to this host or IP, overriding DNS for the initial configuration request.

examples.desc: Test one interface only and save the JSON
See which fields the JSON contains before you parse it

gotchas: The test uses a lot of bandwidth for its duration. On metered or tethered connections, think first.
Results from a Mac on Wi-Fi measure your Wi-Fi link plus the internet. To isolate the internet, repeat the test over Ethernet or `-I` another interface.

blocks.text: Run `ping -c 20 1.1.1.1` in one tab and `networkQuality` in another at the same time. Watch the ping times climb while the test saturates the link. The size of that climb is the bufferbloat, and it is why responsiveness is reported separately from capacity.
Common mistakes

items.text: **Treating a failed ping as a dead host.** Filtering ICMP is common. Confirm with a TCP test.
**Reading one traceroute hop as the truth.** Per-hop times include the router's own delay. Look at the trend and use `mtr` for loss.
**Alarm over `* * *`.** Judge by whether later hops answer.
**Using Linux flags on macOS.** `ping -W 2` and `ping -w 5` mean different things; `traceroute -w` is seconds, `ping -W` is milliseconds.
**Averaging without looking.** One 900 ms outlier among 100 samples moves the mean; report p95 and max too.
**Comparing tests made on different interfaces.** Wi-Fi to Ethernet differs by more than the internet does. Name the interface in every result.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Loss from a saved run

task.text: From `ping.log` in the lab, print only the packet loss percentage (for example `10.0%`), then separately count how many probes timed out using a different pattern. Both numbers must agree.

hints: The statistics line contains the word `loss`. Percent is field 7 on that line.
blocks.solution:
awk '/packet loss/ {print $7}' ping.log
grep -c 'Request timeout' ping.log

why.text: `awk` with a pattern selects one line and prints one field. The loss line says 10.0 percent of 10 packets, and exactly one `Request timeout` line exists, so the two views agree.

blocks.title: Five numbers from ping.log

task.text: Print `n`, `min`, `avg`, `max` and `p95` for the reply times in `ping.log` on one line each or as one summary line. Do not use the statistics line already printed by ping; compute from the individual replies.

hints: Sort numerically, then use `v[NR]` and `END` for the percentile; sums and counts need no sort.
blocks.solution: awk -F'[= ]' '/time=/ {print $(NF-1)}' ping.log | sort -n | awk '{v[NR]=$1; s+=$1} END {p=int(0.95*NR); if (p<0.95*NR) p++; printf "n=%d min=%.3f avg=%.3f max=%.3f p95=%.3f\n", NR, v[1], s/NR, v[NR], v[p]}'

why.text: After sorting, the first value is the minimum and the last is the maximum. The array lets `END` pick the element at the 95th-percentile rank, and the running sum gives the mean.

blocks.title: Path MTU on purpose

task.text: Break it, then measure it. First run `ping -c 1 -D -s 1473 example.com` and read the error. Then find the largest payload that works to `example.com` by trying sizes, and print the path MTU. Finally say what MTU you would expect from a VPN that shows `mtu 1380` on its `utun` interface.

hints: Payload plus 28 is the packet size. The error `Message too long` is local: the packet exceeds your own MTU.
Try 1472, then smaller values in steps of 20 until one works.

why.text: 1473 + 28 is 1501, one byte over a 1500-byte link, so the kernel refuses to send. If 1472 works the path MTU is 1500. Through a VPN with `mtu 1380`, the largest ping payload is 1380 - 28 = 1352.

blocks.title: Rank your hosts by latency

task.text: For every name in `hosts.txt`, print the average RTT of three pings next to the name, fastest first. Hosts that do not answer must still appear, at the bottom. Remember: `ping -W` is milliseconds and a dead host can take long to give up.

hints: Use a `while read -r h` loop that reads from `hosts.txt`.
Use `${avg:-9999}` so missing values sort last, and `sort -n` at the end.
blocks.solution:
while read -r h; do
  avg=$(ping -c 3 -t 4 -W 1000 "$h" 2>/dev/null | awk -F/ '/round-trip/ {print $5}')
  print "${avg:-9999} $h"
done < hosts.txt | sort -n

why.text: Each loop pass produces one line. A failed ping leaves `avg` empty, so the default `9999` pushes it to the end after the numeric sort. `-t 4` guarantees the loop cannot hang on a dead host.

blocks.title: Where does it get slow?

task.text: Here is a trace from a laptop in a cafe to a web server.

items.text: Is the silent hop 2 a fault?
Where does the latency first become large, and is it persistent?
What does hop 6 tell you?
Which tool would you run next to decide whether any packets are being lost?

blocks.solution:
1. No. Traffic gets through to hop 3 and beyond, so hop 2 only declines to answer.
2. At hop 3 (3.2 ms to 48.6 ms) and it stays at about 50 ms to the end, so there is a persistent extra delay of about 45 ms after the first hop. That is typical of a mobile or shared uplink such as a phone hotspot (172.20.10.x) and CGNAT (100.64.x.x).
3. Hop 6 spikes to 189 ms but hops 7 and 8 are back to 54 ms. The router at hop 6 is slow to *answer* ICMP; it forwards normally, so it is not the problem.
4. `sudo mtr -rwnc 30 198.51.100.20`, looking at loss at the final hop.

why.text: Persistent increases that carry through to the destination reflect real delay on the path. A spike at a single hop that disappears afterwards is router control-plane delay. Silence is not loss unless it continues to the end.

blocks.title: Break the timeout

task.text: `192.0.2.1` is in the TEST-NET-1 documentation range and is never routed on the internet. Ping it with `ping -c 2 -t 4 192.0.2.1`, then print the exit status. Then ping a name that does not exist, such as `nohost.invalid`, and print that exit status. Explain the two numbers.

hints: `echo $?` immediately after the command shows its exit status.

why.text: The first run sends packets that nobody answers and exits with status 2 ("sent, no reply"). The second fails before sending anything because the name does not resolve, so ping reports an error, status 68 on macOS. A script can tell "unreachable" from "mistyped name" by the status.

options.text: A wait of 1000 milliseconds for each reply

questions.why: On macOS `-W` is the per-reply wait in milliseconds. Linux uses seconds for the same flag, a common source of copy-paste errors.

questions.q: A traceroute shows `* * *` at hop 5 but hops 6 and 7 answer normally. What is the most likely meaning?

options.text: The path is broken at hop 5
Hop 5 forwards traffic but does not send time-exceeded replies

questions.why: Later hops answer, so traffic passes through hop 5. The router just does not send, or rate-limits, ICMP time-exceeded messages.

questions.q: What payload size gives a full 1500-byte packet in `ping -D -s SIZE`?
questions.why: 1500 minus 20 bytes of IP header and 8 bytes of ICMP header is 1472.

questions.q: In an mtr report, hop 4 shows 60 percent loss but the last hop shows 0 percent. What do you conclude?

options.text: Real packet loss on the path
Hop 4 rate-limits ICMP replies; the traffic itself is not being lost

questions.why: Loss that does not continue to the final hop means the router declines to answer probes, not that your packets disappear.

questions.q: Which command computes the average RTT from ping's summary line?
questions.why: The summary line reads `round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = a/b/c/d ms`. Splitting on `/` makes the average the fifth field.

questions.q: Why does `sort` need `-n` when ranking RTTs?

options.text: Without it numbers sort as text, so 9.5 comes after 12.3

questions.why: Text sort compares character by character, so a leading 9 beats a leading 1. `-n` compares numeric values.

blocks.text: Build a recorder and a summariser. The recorder appends one line per probe to a CSV; the summariser turns a CSV into the numbers you would give an ISP. Leave the recorder running during a work session and you will have evidence of when the connection degrades.
Step 1: The recorder

Create `~/lab/latency-log.zsh`. It writes a header once, then loops: take a timestamp, send one ping, extract the time (or the word `timeout`), append a CSV line, wait. The `-t 2` guarantees one dead probe cannot stall the loop.

blocks.code: chmod +x latency-log.zsh && ./latency-log.zsh {{host}} 12 2 latency.csv && tail -5 latency.csv

blocks.text: `${rtt:-timeout}` writes the word `timeout` when the pipeline produced nothing. The same marker appears for an unresolvable name, so check that `{{host}}` works with a plain `ping` first.
Step 2: The summariser
The summariser has two jobs. Loss is the share of `timeout` rows. The statistics come from the numeric rows, which need sorting for the percentile.
Step 3: Test it on data you already have
Before trusting the summariser on live data, feed it the saved lab ping run. This converts `ping.log` into the same CSV shape, so you know the expected answer (9 replies, 1 timeout, average 12.939).

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ echo "timestamp,host,rtt_ms" > test.csv
$ awk -F'[= ]' '/time=/ {print "2026-10-08T09:00:00,example.com," $(NF-1)} /timeout/ {print "2026-10-08T09:00:00,example.com,timeout"}' ping.log >> test.csv
$ head -4 test.csv
timestamp,host,rtt_ms
2026-10-08T09:00:00,example.com,11.842
2026-10-08T09:00:00,example.com,12.310
2026-10-08T09:00:00,example.com,11.205
$ awk -F, 'NR>1 {t++} NR>1 && $3=="timeout" {l++} END {printf "probes=%d lost=%d loss=%.1f%%\n", t, l, (t ? 100*l/t : 0)}' test.csv
probes=10 lost=1 loss=10.0%
$ awk -F, 'NR>1 && $3!="timeout" {print $3}' test.csv | sort -n | awk '{v[NR]=$1; s+=$1} END {p=int(0.95*NR); if (p<0.95*NR) p++; printf "n=%d min=%.2f avg=%.2f p95=%.2f max=%.2f ms\n", NR, v[1], s/NR, v[p], v[NR]}'
n=9 min=11.21 avg=12.94 p95=16.10 max=16.10 ms

blocks.text: Step 4: Run it for real

Record 20 minutes of a host you care about (your gateway, then a public service), then compare the summaries. If the gateway looks clean and the public host does not, the problem is beyond your router.

blocks.code:
./latency-log.zsh {{gateway}} 240 5 gw.csv &
./latency-log.zsh {{host}} 240 5 web.csv &
wait
./latency-summary.zsh gw.csv && ./latency-summary.zsh web.csv

blocks.text: Add a `jitter` line using the consecutive-difference formula from this chapter. Make the recorder write a `SLOW` flag when the RTT exceeds a threshold given as a fifth argument. Run it from `launchd` so it starts on login ([Scripting](#scripting) covers the plist).
Try it in the practice terminal

The practice terminal can run `ping` and `traceroute` against the lab network and `awk` over `ping.log`, so every statistics pipeline in this chapter works there. Try ranking the lab router, the Pi and the NAS by their ping averages.
Next

You can tell whether a host is reachable and how the path behaves. Continue to [DNS](#dns), where you turn names into addresses, read every record type and learn why "the internet is down" is so often a DNS problem.

terms.def: The ICMP request/reply pair (types 8 and 0) that ping uses
The time between sending a probe and receiving its reply
The share of probes or packets that never arrive
The value below which a given share of the samples fall; p95 means 95 percent are at or below it
One router between a source and a destination
The ICMP message (type 11) a router sends when it drops a packet whose TTL reached zero
The smallest MTU on any link between two hosts
An IP header bit telling routers to drop the packet rather than split it
Excess latency under load caused by oversized queues in network equipment
Apple's measure of round trips per minute while the link is saturated
Round-trips per minute: the unit of responsiveness in networkQuality
Forward and return traffic taking different paths
